reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: A hydrocele is a collection of serous fluid within the tunica vaginalis, presenting as a painless, fluctuant scrotal swelling that transilluminates brightly
A key examination finding is the ability to get above the swelling, distinguishing it from an inguinoscrotal hernia, and the testis is often impalpable within a large tension hydrocele
In infants, communicating hydroceles arise from a patent processus vaginalis and commonly resolve spontaneously within the first year or two of life
Adult hydroceles are usually idiopathic (primary) but may be secondary to underlying pathology such as tumour, infection, trauma, or torsion, so the testis must be assessed
Ultrasound is indicated when the testis cannot be palpated or when a secondary cause is suspected, to exclude an underlying testicular tumour
A rapidly developing or blood-stained hydrocele after trauma or in a young man should prompt evaluation for testicular malignancy or haematocele

Treatment principles include observation for asymptomatic cases, with surgical repair (hydrocelectomy) preferred for large or symptomatic adult hydroceles and aspiration reserved for those unfit for surgery due to high recurrence
In children, persistent or symptomatic hydroceles beyond infancy are managed by ligation of the patent processus via an inguinal approach
reference.pathophysiology: A hydrocele results from an imbalance between secretion and absorption of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Congenital (communicating) hydroceles occur when the processus vaginalis fails to obliterate, allowing peritoneal fluid to track into the scrotum. Non-communicating hydroceles arise from excess fluid production or impaired reabsorption by the tunica. Secondary hydroceles develop as a reactive effusion in response to underlying testicular or epididymal disease such as tumour, infection, torsion, or trauma. Chronic large hydroceles may occasionally impair testicular perfusion or spermatogenesis.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound when the testis is impalpable or a secondary cause is suspected
Assessment for underlying infection, trauma, or torsion as clinically indicated
Tumour markers if testicular malignancy is a concern on imaging
redFlags: An impalpable testis within the hydrocele, mandating ultrasound to exclude tumour
Rapidly enlarging, tense, or blood-stained (haematocele) swelling following trauma
A reactive hydrocele masking an underlying testicular malignancy
Signs of associated infection or torsion requiring urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: Infantile communicating hydroceles usually resolve spontaneously; primary adult hydroceles are benign and surgery is generally curative, whereas the outlook of secondary hydroceles depends on the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Assuming a scrotal swelling is a simple hydrocele without confirming a normal underlying testis
Aspirating an adult hydrocele as definitive treatment, given the high recurrence and risk of missing tumour
Failing to recognise a reactive hydrocele overlying a testicular tumour
Confusing a hydrocele with an inguinoscrotal hernia when unable to get above the swelling
Operating on infantile hydroceles prematurely before allowing spontaneous resolution
management: Conservative observation for infantile communicating hydroceles, most of which resolve spontaneously within the first year or two of life
Surgical ligation of the patent processus vaginalis for communicating hydroceles that persist beyond early childhood
Reassurance and observation of small, asymptomatic primary adult hydroceles
Surgical repair such as the Jaboulay or Lord procedure for symptomatic or large primary hydroceles, with aspiration and sclerotherapy reserved for those unfit for surgery
Identification and treatment of any underlying cause in secondary hydroceles, such as infection, trauma, or torsion
Scrotal ultrasound and, where indicated, tumour markers to exclude an underlying testicular malignancy before treating a suspected secondary hydrocele
